cover.title: Docker Complete Handbook
cover.subtitle: From Basics to Advanced
cover.tagline: What it is, why it ends 'works on my machine', and the 15-page roadmap

items: The `docker` CLI is only a client; ==dockerd== is the daemon, talking over a **REST API**
Default socket `/var/run/docker.sock`; `DOCKER_HOST=ssh://user@host` aims the CLI at a remote daemon
A saved `docker context` switches daemons in one command
`docker info` shows the storage driver, usually ==overlay2==
The shim lets a container outlive a `dockerd` restart; `runc` follows the **OCI** spec, so runtimes are swappable
Tip: `docker top <c>` and host `ps` show the container's process is just a normal host process

rows: pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user

blocks.title: Mistake: mounting docker.sock
blocks.text: `-v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock` hands the container **root-equivalent** control of the host.

blocks.title: Interview Point
items: Walk through what happens on `docker run`.
How do namespaces differ from cgroups?
Why does Docker use containerd and runc?
Is a container a lightweight VM?
KEY TAKEAWAYS: CLI → dockerd → containerd → shim → runc: namespaces isolate, cgroups limit, one shared kernel.
An ==image== is an immutable, layered filesystem plus metadata
Metadata holds config, `ENTRYPOINT`, `CMD` and `ENV`
Read-only: running it never edits the image
Container = image + a thin writable layer on top
`RUN`, `COPY` and `ADD` each create a ==layer==
Every layer is addressed by its **SHA256** digest
Same content gives the same digest, so layers are shared
Shared layers are cached: less disk, faster pulls
A ==manifest== lists the config blob and layer digests
A manifest list (index) maps platforms to manifests
`amd64` and `arm64` hosts pull their own variant
One tag, many architectures

blocks.note: Sizes sum to the image size

items: Relying on `latest`: it moves without warning, builds drift
Deleting a file in a later layer: the earlier layer still holds it
Fix: pin a tag or digest, and delete in the same `RUN`
Fix: multi-stage builds ship only the final artifact

blocks.title: Tip: Spot Fat Layers
blocks.text: Run `docker history <image>` and look for one huge row: that step is your shrink target.

blocks.title: Interview Point
items: What is a layer and how is it cached?
Tag vs digest: which is safer to deploy?
How does a multi-arch image work?
How do you shrink an image?

blocks.title: KEY TAKEAWAYS:
blocks.text: Images are immutable stacks of shared, digest-addressed layers: pin by digest and never expect a later delete to shrink them.

items: A ==container== is a running (or stopped) instance of an image
An isolated process with its own filesystem, network and process tree
States: created, running, paused, exited, removed

blocks.text: Add `--rm` to **auto-remove** the container the moment it exits.

items: `--memory=512m` and `--cpus=1.5` are enforced by ==cgroups==
Exceed memory: process is OOM-killed, exit code **137**
`--restart` picks a restart policy (see table)

rows: any exit, also on daemon start

items: The main process is ==PID 1==
When PID 1 exits, the container exits
`docker exec` starts a **new** process in a running container
`docker attach` connects to PID 1's stdio

slides.page_title: ENTRYPOINT vs CMD and Exit Codes

items: Shell-form CMD makes `sh` PID 1: SIGTERM never reaches your app
Fix: exec form `CMD ["node","app.js"]`, or run with `--init`
Result: `docker stop` hangs 10s, then SIGKILL

blocks.title: Tip: Confirm an OOM kill
blocks.text: `docker inspect --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}}' web` prints true when the memory cap killed it.

items: `docker stats` shows live memory against the cap
`docker ps -a` lists exited containers and codes
`docker logs web` shows the last output

blocks.title: Interview Point
blocks.text: What happens on docker stop? Why does a container exit immediately? ENTRYPOINT vs CMD? What does exit code 137 mean?

blocks.title: Key Takeaways:
blocks.text: A container lives and dies with PID 1, so signals, limits and restart policy decide its fate.

slides.subtitle: Run, limit, stop

items: A ==Dockerfile== is a text recipe of ordered instructions
`docker build` turns it into an image
`FROM` picks the base image; `WORKDIR` sets and creates the working dir
`COPY` copies from the build context; `ADD` also extracts local tars and fetches URLs
`RUN` runs at build time and creates a layer; `CMD` and `ENTRYPOINT` define runtime behavior
`ENV` persists in image and container; `ARG` is __build-time only__
`EXPOSE 3000` only ==documents== a port; `-p 8080:3000` publishes it
`USER node` switches off root; `HEALTHCHECK` is a liveness probe command
`LABEL` attaches metadata; `VOLUME` declares a mount point
`STOPSIGNAL` sets the signal sent on stop

slides.page_title: Dockerfile Forms and a Node Example

blocks.title: Tip: Build and Run It
blocks.text: `docker build -t app .` then `docker run -p 8080:3000 app` publishes the port that `EXPOSE` only documents.

items: Secrets in `ENV` or `ARG` stay readable in `docker history` and `image inspect`
Shell-form `CMD` hides your app from SIGTERM
Assuming `EXPOSE` makes a port reachable

blocks.title: Interview Point
items: ARG vs ENV: build-only or persisted?
COPY vs ADD: when is ADD justified?
What does EXPOSE actually do?
CMD vs ENTRYPOINT in a Dockerfile?

blocks.title: KEY TAKEAWAYS:
blocks.text: Prefer COPY, exec-form CMD, USER node, and never put secrets in ENV or ARG.

slides.subtitle: The image recipe

items: The ==build cache== reuses a layer when its instruction and inputs are unchanged
Inputs = the instruction text plus the files `COPY` reads
**Cascade**: once one layer changes, every layer after it rebuilds
Order from least to most frequently changing: ==dependencies first==, source last
Copy only the manifest (`package.json`, `go.mod`, `requirements.txt`) before installing
`.dockerignore` shrinks the context; keeps `node_modules`, `.git`, `.env` out
Several `FROM` lines; `COPY --from=builder` ships only the ==final artifact==
Build stages hold compilers and dev tools
The runtime stage holds only the binary and runtime

rows: credential not left in a layer

blocks.note: secret never lands in a layer

slides.page_title: Multi-Stage Go Build and Cache Pitfalls

blocks.title: Tip: Read the Cache
blocks.text: `docker build --progress=plain .` marks reused steps CACHED; add `--no-cache` to rule out a stale layer.

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: Rarely changing layers go first, often changing layers last.

items: `FROM golang:1.23 AS build` names a stage
`COPY --from=build` can pull from any earlier stage
`--target build` stops the build at that stage

blocks.title: Tip: Debug One Stage
blocks.text: `docker build --target build -t dbg .` builds only up to that stage, so you can inspect its tools.

items: `COPY . .` before installing deps busts the cache on every code change
Separate `RUN apt-get update` and `install` layers leave a stale cache
Combine them and clean `/var/lib/apt/lists`
Secrets passed as `ARG` or `COPY` stay in a layer; use a secret mount

blocks.title: Interview Point
blocks.text: Why does instruction order matter? How do multi-stage builds cut image size? What is BuildKit? How do you pass secrets safely at build time?

blocks.title: KEY TAKEAWAYS:
blocks.text: Stable layers first, build in one stage, ship only the artifact.

slides.subtitle: Faster, smaller images

items: The container's ==writable layer== is deleted with the container
{green:**Volumes**}: Docker-managed storage in `/var/lib/docker/volumes`
{blue:**Bind mounts**} map a host path in, tied to the host's layout
{orange:**tmpfs**} lives in host memory only: sensitive or scratch data
`--mount` is explicit and **errors** on a missing path
`-v` silently **creates** a missing host directory
`ro` flag makes the mount read-only
Volume drivers (local, NFS, cloud plugins) reach remote storage
A new empty named volume is ==populated== from the image's content; a bind mount **hides** it

blocks.title: Tip: Find Where Data Lives
blocks.text: `docker volume inspect pgdata` prints the Mountpoint under `/var/lib/docker/volumes`, handy for checking size.

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: Databases get a named volume, dev code gets a bind mount, secrets get tmpfs.

blocks.note: throwaway container writes tar to host

lines: docker run -d -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16  # rows still there

items: `docker volume prune` or `system prune --volumes` silently deletes unused data volumes
`-v $PWD:/app` **hides** the files built into the image
No mount at all: data dies on `docker rm`

blocks.title: KEY TAKEAWAYS:
blocks.text: Containers are disposable: named volumes for data, bind mounts for dev, tmpfs for secrets. Restore: mount volume read-write, run `tar xzf /backup/pg.tgz -C /data`.

blocks.title: Interview Point
items: Volume vs bind mount: when would you use each?
How do you persist database data, and where is data written by default?
How do you back up a volume?

blocks.text: Every container gets its own ==network namespace==, a virtual interface and an IP address.

items: Bridge is the default: containers talk via virtual switch ==docker0==
==User-defined== bridges resolve containers **by name**
The default bridge has no name DNS, only IPs
Different user-defined networks cannot reach each other
Attach a container to both networks to bridge them

blocks.note: name db resolves via embedded DNS

items: `-p 5432:5432` on a database exposes it to the whole network
Docker's iptables rules bypass many host firewalls (ufw)
`localhost` inside a container is the container itself, not the host or another service

blocks.title: Tip: Check the Wiring
blocks.text: `docker network inspect app` lists attached containers and IPs; `docker port web` shows published ports.

items: `docker network ls` lists all networks
`docker network connect app web` attaches a running container
`docker network disconnect app web` detaches it

a_bullets: How do containers find each other by name?
Why can't a container reach default-bridge peers by name?

blocks.title: KEY TAKEAWAYS:
blocks.text: Use user-defined networks for name DNS, and publish only the ports you must, bound to 127.0.0.1 when private.

items: One ==compose.yaml== defines a multi-container app; `docker compose up` runs it
Top-level keys: `services`, `networks`, `volumes`, `configs`, `secrets`
A service sets `image` or `build`, `ports`, `environment`, `volumes`
Also `depends_on`, `restart` and `healthcheck`
Compose makes a ==default network== per project
Services reach each other by __service name__: `db:5432`
`depends_on` alone only **orders** startup, not readiness
`condition: service_healthy` waits for the healthcheck

blocks.title: Tip: Layer a Prod File
blocks.text: `docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml up -d` merges the later file over the earlier one.

blocks.title: Tip: Preview the Merged Config
blocks.text: `docker compose config` prints the final YAML after overrides and `.env` interpolation; `--profile debug up` starts the optional services.

blocks.note: named volume pgdata keeps the data

blocks.title: 4. Core commands
items: `up -d` starts detached; `down` stops and removes
`ps`, `logs -f`, `exec` inspect and enter a service
`build` rebuilds images; `config` prints merged YAML
`watch` syncs or rebuilds on save: fast dev loop

blocks.note: plain depends_on skips the health wait

blocks.title: 7. Mistake
items: `docker compose down -v` deletes named volumes
The data inside them is gone for good
Use plain `down` to keep pgdata

slides.page_title: Compose down vs stop and Rebuilds

blocks.title: Tip: Rebuild One Service
blocks.text: `docker compose up -d --build web` rebuilds and recreates only `web`; `db` keeps running.

blocks.title: KEY TAKEAWAYS:
blocks.text: One file, one network, healthy-gated startup: ideal on a single host, not multi-host production.

blocks.title: Interview Point
items: What does depends_on guarantee?
How do services discover each other?
How do you manage dev vs prod config?
Is Compose production-ready?

slides.subtitle: Multi-container apps

items: A ==registry== stores and serves images over HTTP
A **repository** holds the versions (tags) of one image
`nginx` is the repository; `1.27` and `latest` are tags
Docker Hub is the ==default registry== when none is named
`docker login` saves credentials in `~/.docker/config.json`
Plain text there is just base64, not encryption
Set a ==credential helper== (`credsStore`) to use the OS keychain
In CI, pipe a token with `--password-stdin`

caption.text:
Everything you need before your Docker interview, in one handbook. 🐳

From how the engine works under the hood to shipping containers in production, this is the whole Docker story written out as handwritten notes you can swipe through and actually remember.

✅ Docker Architecture and Engine Internals

✅ Containers and the Lifecycle
✅ Dockerfile Essentials
✅ Build Cache and Multi-Stage Builds
✅ Volumes and Storage
✅ Docker Networking
✅ Docker Compose
✅ Registries and Image Distribution
✅ Container Security
✅ Debugging and Troubleshooting
✅ Production and Orchestration
✅ Best Practices and Common Mistakes
✅ Docker Interview Questions
✅ Docker Cheatsheet

Who it's for: developers, DevOps beginners and anyone preparing for backend or DevOps interviews who wants Docker to finally click, start to finish.

Save this so you have it when the interview invite lands, and send it to the teammate who still says "it works on my machine."

Comment “docker” and I’ll send you the full PDF.
